title: End-to-End and Visual Tests
summary: Test whole user journeys in a real browser with Playwright 1.64, control the network and logins, catch visual regressions, and debug failures.
intro: Unit and component tests swap the browser for jsdom and the API for MSW. That makes them fast, and it means they can't see some bugs: a CSS rule that hides the Add to cart button, a proxy setting that sends requests to the wrong place, a cookie the real API sets differently than the mock. End-to-end tests run the real, built app in a real browser against a real server, and click through it the way a shopper does. This lesson tests the shop's key journeys with Playwright: what such a test proves, how to set it up, how to find things and wait for them, how to control the network and log in once, how to catch visual changes with screenshots, and how to debug a failure and run it all in CI.

steps.title: What an end-to-end test proves
steps.body:
Every test so far has faked something. An end-to-end test fakes as little as possible, so when it passes, the journey works the way a shopper would really meet it. That's the strongest proof a test can give, and the most expensive one, so it's worth knowing exactly what it buys.

## Everything real

An end-to-end test, or **e2e** test, from the levels in Unit and Component Tests, runs:

- **A real browser.** Chromium, the open-source core of Chrome, with real layout, real CSS, real focus and scrolling. A button covered by another element can't be clicked, just as for a person.
- **The real build.** `npm run build`, then `vite preview` serving `dist/`, so the test checks what you'll ship: the bundle, the proxy, the routes, the SPA fallback.
- **A real server.** The Trailhead API, running with its seed data, setting real cookies and answering with real status codes.

```diagram e2e-and-visual-tests-stack
The test drives a browser, which loads the built app, which calls the API. Only the test is new.
```

In the diagram, the test runner, on the left, drives Chromium as a person would. Chromium loads the shop from `vite preview`, and the shop's `/v1` requests go through the preview server's proxy to the API. Nothing in that chain is a stand-in.

## Journeys

E2e tests check **journeys**: the paths through the app that people take to get something done. For a shop, those are the ones that make money or lose it: logging in, finding a product, adding it to the cart, checking out. One test walks a whole journey, across several pages, and checks what the shopper sees at each step. The first example is one: open the shop, pick the Storm Shell Jacket, add two, and see them in the cart with the right total.

## Fewer, slower, and the most realistic

Each e2e test takes from a fraction of a second to several seconds, against milliseconds for a component test, since a browser has to start, load pages, and wait for a server. They're also harder to keep reliable, since more moving parts means more ways for timing to vary. So the trophy from Unit and Component Tests keeps them few: one test per important journey, plus the failures that only a real browser can show. The details, like every error message, stay in component tests, where they're cheap.

## Playwright's pieces

**Playwright** is a tool for driving browsers from code, made by Microsoft. Its test runner, `@playwright/test`, is what this lesson uses. Four words come up constantly:

- **The runner** finds the test files, starts the servers, runs the tests in parallel, and reports.
- **A browser** is one engine: Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit, the engine inside Safari. One config can run every test in each.
- **A context** is like a fresh browser profile: its own cookies, its own `localStorage`, its own cache. Every test gets a new one, so one test's login or cart never leaks into another, and making one takes milliseconds.
- **A page** is one tab inside a context. Most tests use the one `page` they're given.

examples.title: A shopper's journey
examples.prompt: `e2e/checkout.spec.ts`, in an `e2e/` folder at the root of the shop, outside `src/`.
examples.explanation: Each test gets `page` from Playwright. `test.use` at the top makes every test in the file start logged in as Sam, which part 4 sets up. The first test is the whole journey: from the product list, follow the Storm Shell Jacket link, check the URL and the heading, type a quantity, add it, wait for the status message, open the cart, and check the line and the subtotal. Every step is something a shopper does or sees. The second is a failure only the real API knows about: Hip Pack 5L has no stock in the seed data, so the API answers 409, and the page says how many are left.

steps.title: Setting up Playwright
steps.body:
Playwright needs three things before a test can run: the runner, a browser, and servers for the browser to talk to. One config file ties them together, so a single command starts everything, runs the tests, and stops it again.

## Installing

Add the runner as a dev dependency, then download a browser for it:

```bash
npm install -D @playwright/test
npx playwright install chromium
```

`playwright install` downloads Playwright's own build of Chromium, about 100 MB, into a cache folder on your computer that all your projects share. Each version of Playwright expects a matching browser, so run it again after you upgrade. `npx playwright install` with no name gets Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. On a Linux machine, like a CI server, `--with-deps` also installs the system libraries the browsers need.

`npm init playwright@latest` does all of this for a new project and writes a starter config, if you'd rather start from that.

## The config

`playwright.config.ts` at the project's root is the first example. These are its parts:

- `testDir` is where the tests live, `e2e/`. Vitest's config only looks in `src/`, so the two runners never pick up each other's files.
- `fullyParallel` runs every test at the same time, in separate **workers**, each its own process with its own browser.
- `forbidOnly` fails the run in CI if someone left a `test.only`, which runs one test and skips the rest, in a commit.
- `retries` runs a failed test again, twice in CI and never on your computer. Part 6 explains why.
- `reporter` chooses how results are shown: a line per test locally, plus an HTML report, and annotations on the pull request in GitHub's CI.
- `use` sets options for every test. `baseURL` lets tests write `page.goto("/cart")`. `trace` records a step-by-step trace of a test when it's retried, for debugging.
- `projects` are named groups of tests with their own settings. Here, `setup` logs in once, and `chromium` runs everything else after it. Adding a `firefox` project would run the same tests in Firefox too.

## Starting the servers

`webServer` is a list of commands Playwright runs before the tests, waiting until each `url` answers, and stops afterward. The shop needs two:

1. The Trailhead API, from the `trailhead-api` folder next to the shop, on its own port, 4010, so tests never touch the data you're using on 4000 while you work. `TRAILHEAD_TEST=1` turns on a reset endpoint that only tests use.
2. The shop itself, built and served with `vite preview` on port 4173. `API_URL` points the preview server's proxy at the test API instead of the usual one, which is why `vite.config.ts` reads it. `VITE_API_URL=/v1` makes the build call `/v1` on its own origin, as the dev server does. Without it, the build would bake in the real API's address from `.env.production`, and the tests would leave your computer.

`reuseExistingServer` lets you start the servers yourself and keep them running between runs on your computer, which saves the build time. In CI it's off, so every run starts fresh.

Add `"e2e": "playwright test"` to the scripts, and `test-results`, `playwright-report`, and `e2e/.auth` to `.gitignore`: they're outputs, and the last one holds a login.

## Running it

`npx playwright test` starts the servers, runs the tests, and prints a line per test, as the second example shows. `npx playwright test e2e/checkout.spec.ts` runs one file, and `-g "sold-out"` runs the tests whose names match.

examples.title: The Playwright config
examples.prompt: `playwright.config.ts`, at the root of the shop.
examples.explanation: `process.env.CI` is set by CI services like GitHub Actions, so the config can behave differently there: retries on, `test.only` forbidden, servers always fresh, and the `github` reporter instead of the list. `devices["Desktop Chrome"]` is a ready-made set of options: the window size, the user agent, and the scale of a desktop Chrome. `dependencies: ["setup"]` means the chromium project waits until the setup project has passed. The `env` on each server sets environment variables for that command only, and the comment says why the shop's build needs two. The API's `url` is a real endpoint, since Playwright waits for it to answer before any test starts.

examples.title: Running every test
examples.explanation: Eight tests ran on seven workers: the setup first, alone, since everything else depends on it, then the other seven at once, which is why they finish out of order. Each line names the project in brackets, the file and line, the test's name, and its time. Most took about half a second or less. The slowest, at 7.7 seconds, waits for the app to give up on a failing API, which part 4 explains. The whole run took about eleven seconds. The HTML report is in `playwright-report/`, and `npx playwright show-report` opens it.

steps.title: Locators, actions, and assertions
steps.body:
A browser is slower and less predictable than jsdom: pages load, requests take time, animations run. Most flaky e2e tests come from checking too early. Playwright's locators and assertions are built to wait the right amount, as long as you let them.

## Locators

A **locator** describes how to find an element: `page.getByRole("button", { name: "Add Storm Shell Jacket to cart" })`. It doesn't search right away. It searches each time you use it, so it always finds the element as the page is now, even after React has replaced it. The methods mirror Testing Library's, in the same order of preference:

- `page.getByRole(role, { name })` first, for the same reasons: it's what a person sees, and what a screen reader uses.
- `page.getByLabel("Quantity")` for form fields.
- `page.getByText("Subtotal: $438.00")` for text that isn't a control.
- `page.getByTestId("...")` as the last resort.

A locator that matches several elements is an error when you act on it, which catches mistakes like clicking the wrong one of two Add buttons. Narrow it with `.first()`, `.last()`, or by searching inside another locator: `page.getByRole("navigation").getByRole("link", { name: "Cart" })`.

## Actions and auto-waiting

`click()`, `fill("2")`, `press("Enter")`, `check()`, `selectOption("3")`, and `pressSequentially("tent")`, which types one key at a time like a person, are the actions you'll use most. Before each action, Playwright **auto-waits**: it waits until the element exists, is visible, has stopped moving, is enabled, and isn't covered by something else, then acts. So clicking a button that appears after a request just works, with no waiting code. If the element never gets there, the action fails after a timeout, with a message saying which check it was stuck on.

## Assertions that retry

`await expect(locator).toHaveText("Added to your cart.")` is a **web-first assertion**: it keeps checking the page until the text matches, for up to five seconds, and only then fails. Note the `await`: without it, the test moves on before the check finishes. These are the ones you'll use most:

- `toBeVisible()`, `toBeHidden()`, `toBeEnabled()`, `toBeDisabled()`.
- `toHaveText(...)` for the whole text, or `toContainText(...)` for part of it.
- `toHaveValue(...)` for a field, `toHaveCount(n)` for how many elements match.
- `expect(page).toHaveURL("/products/storm-shell-jacket")` and `toHaveTitle(...)` for the page itself.

Plain `expect(value).toBe(...)`, without a locator, checks once and doesn't retry, like Vitest's. Use it for values you already have, like a response's status.

## No sleeps

`page.waitForTimeout(2000)` pauses for two seconds no matter what. It's too long when the app is fast, which slows every run, and too short when the CI server is busy, which makes the test flaky. Wait for something you can see instead: a web-first assertion, or a response, which part 4 covers. Keep `waitForTimeout` for poking at a page while you debug.

## Fixtures

The `{ page }` in each test's arguments is a **fixture**: something Playwright sets up before the test and cleans up after, handed in by name. `page` and `context` give the test a fresh tab in a fresh context. `request` makes API calls with no browser, which is handy for setup. `browserName` says which project is running. You ask for what you need, and only that is set up.

The example is a journey across three pages, with a login in the middle.

examples.title: A guest's cart follows them in
examples.prompt: `e2e/guest.spec.ts`. No `test.use`, so the test starts logged out, like a first-time visitor. It logs in as Ana, so its cart never meets the cart Sam's tests fill.
examples.explanation: The guest adds two jackets, and the header's link changes to Cart (2) with no request to the API, since a guest's cart is the Zustand store from the Sharing State lesson, saved in the browser. `toBeVisible` on a link named exactly Cart (2) waits for that. Then the test logs in through the real form. Logging in copies the guest cart to Ana's account on the server and empties the browser's copy, so after Hi, Ana appears, the cart page lists the jacket with a line total the API worked out. Every link is found by its role and its full name, and each assertion waits for its page, so the test needs no waiting code of its own.

steps.title: Network control and logging in
steps.body:
A real API is the point of e2e tests, but you still need control over it. Some cases can't be produced on demand, like the API failing, and some setup, like logging in, would make every test slow if each did it through the form. Playwright handles both.

## Routing requests

`page.route(url, handler)` catches the page's requests whose URL matches, before they leave the browser, and lets the handler decide:

- `route.fulfill({ status, contentType, body })` answers without asking the server, as a **stub**.
- `route.continue()` sends the request on, so you can delay it first, or change its headers.
- `route.abort()` fails it, as if the network were down.

The URL is a glob pattern, where `*` matches anything but a `/`, and `**` matches anything at all. `"**/v1/products*"` matches the product list with or without a query string, but not `/v1/products/storm-shell-jacket`, which has another `/`. The first example uses `page.route` for the two cases the real API won't give you: an error, and a slow answer.

The error test taught the team something about their own app. With the usual five-second timeout, it failed: the page still said Loading products…. TanStack Query, by default, retries a failed request three times, waiting about 1, 2, and 4 seconds, before it reports an error. So the test waits up to ten seconds for the alert, with a comment saying why. Part 6 shows the failure.

Routing is for the cases you can't produce otherwise. If most of your e2e tests stub the API, they've become slower component tests.

## Waiting for a response

`page.waitForResponse(predicate)` waits for a response that matches. Start waiting before the action that triggers it, or the response could arrive before you're listening:

```ts
const search = page.waitForResponse((response) => response.url().includes("q=tent"));
await page.getByLabel("Search").pressSequentially("tent");
const response = await search;
```

The third test in the example uses this to check that the search box, which waits until typing stops, makes one request for the whole word, not one per letter.

## Logging in once

Logging in through the form in every test would add a second or more to each, and test the login page dozens of times. Instead, a **setup project** logs in once and saves the browser's state, and the other tests start from it. The second example is that setup. `page.context().storageState({ path })` writes the context's cookies and `localStorage` to a JSON file, here `e2e/.auth/sam.json`, which holds Sam's `th_session` cookie. A test file with `test.use({ storageState: "e2e/.auth/sam.json" })` starts each test in a new context loaded from that file, so the shopper is already logged in.

The file holds a real session, so it's in `.gitignore`. To test as two kinds of user, like a shopper and an admin, log in once for each and save two files.

## Starting from known data

Tests that change data, like adding to a cart, can trip over each other, especially in parallel. The shop's tests do three things about it:

- **Reset once.** The setup project calls `POST /__reset` on the test API, which exists only when `TRAILHEAD_TEST=1` is set, so the run starts from the seed data.
- **Don't share.** Each test that writes uses its own product or its own account: Sam's journey adds a Storm Shell Jacket, the sold-out test tries Hip Pack 5L, and the guest's journey logs in as Ana. Tests that only read can share anything.
- **Start fresh in CI.** With `reuseExistingServer` off, each CI run starts its own API, so a run never sees data from the one before.

Bigger apps make a user per test, through the API, so nothing is shared at all.

examples.title: Failing and slow responses
examples.prompt: `e2e/network.spec.ts`, which stubs, delays, and watches the product list.
examples.explanation: The first test answers every product list request with a 500, so the app retries and then shows its alert. The second delays the real response by a second with a `setTimeout` inside the handler, which is the one acceptable place for a fixed wait: it slows the server, not the test. The test then checks the loading message, and the list once it arrives. The third types `tent` a letter at a time, and the search box's 300 millisecond wait means the app asks once, for `q=tent`, which matches the three tents in the seed data.

examples.title: Logging in once, for every test
examples.prompt: `e2e/auth.setup.ts`, which the config's `setup` project runs before the others.
examples.explanation: `test as setup` renames Playwright's `test` so the file reads as setup. The `request` fixture calls the test API's reset endpoint directly, with no browser. Then the page logs in through the real form, the way Sam would, so the setup also checks that logging in works. `toBeVisible` on Hi, Sam waits for the app to finish, since the cookie is set by then. `storageState` writes the cookies and storage to disk. Every test that uses the file skips the form entirely and still makes real, logged-in requests to the API.

steps.title: Visual regression tests
steps.body:
Every test so far checks text, roles, and values. None of them would notice a card that's suddenly twice as wide, a price in white on white, or a button pushed off the screen. Visual tests compare screenshots, so they catch the changes people see first.

## Screenshots as tests

`await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot("products.png")` takes a screenshot and compares it, pixel by pixel, with a saved **baseline**, the approved picture of how the page should look. A test that changes how something looks, on purpose or not, fails until a person looks at the change and approves it.

The first run has no baseline. The test fails, as the first example shows, and writes the screenshot it took as the baseline, in a folder next to the test: `e2e/visual.spec.ts-snapshots/products-chromium-darwin.png`. Look at it, then commit it with the test. From then on, each run compares against it.

When a later change makes the page look different, the test fails with the number of pixels that differ, as the second example shows, and saves three pictures in `test-results/`: the expected one, the actual one, and a **diff**, the expected picture faded out with every changed pixel in red.

```diagram e2e-and-visual-tests-diff
The baseline, the new screenshot, and the diff that marks every pixel that changed.
```

In the diagram, a change of a few pixels of padding moved every card's text. The diff shows exactly where, which is often enough to find the CSS rule. If the change was intended, accept it: `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` writes new baselines, and the commit shows the old and new pictures for review.

## Keeping screenshots stable

A screenshot test is only useful if it's the same every time nothing changed. Anything that varies between runs has to be handled:

- **Animations.** `toHaveScreenshot` stops CSS animations and transitions and hides the text cursor by default, so a half-finished fade can't fail a test.
- **Changing content.** Dates, the cart count, ads, a random tip of the day: `mask: [locator]` covers each matching element with a solid pink box before comparing. The shop masks the header's navigation, which shows the cart count.
- **Small differences.** `maxDiffPixels: 100` or `maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01` let a few pixels differ, for edges that vary by a pixel. Keep these small, or real changes slip through.
- **Data.** Run against seed data, so the page shows the same products every time.

## One machine for every screenshot

The baseline's name ends in `chromium-darwin`: Chromium, on macOS. Fonts, text smoothing, and even colors differ a little between operating systems, so a screenshot taken on a Mac won't match one from Linux, and Playwright keeps separate baselines for each. On a team with Macs, Windows, and a Linux CI server, that's three sets that disagree.

The fix is to take every screenshot on one machine: Playwright's official Docker image, `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright`, tagged with your Playwright version. **Docker** runs a program inside a **container**, a packaged Linux system that's the same wherever it runs. CI runs the tests in that image, as part 6 shows, and teammates update baselines by running the same image on their own computers, so every baseline is a `-linux` one and matches every run.

## Screenshots of one component

Vitest has a **browser mode** that runs component tests in a real browser, through Playwright, instead of jsdom. Its `toMatchScreenshot` takes a screenshot of one element, which is cheaper than a whole page and fails closer to the cause. The third example tests the sold-out card this way. It needs `@vitest/browser-playwright` and `vitest-browser-react`. If npm installs a second, newer `playwright` for them, add `playwright` itself at the same version as `@playwright/test`, or the two ask for different browsers. It also needs a config of its own, `vitest.browser.config.ts`, which sets `browser.enabled` with Chromium and runs files named `*.browser.test.tsx`.

examples.title: A screenshot of the product grid

examples.explanation: The test waits for the product list before the screenshot, so the picture can't catch the loading message. `fullPage: true` captures the whole page, not just the window. The run fails, as every first run does: the error says the snapshot doesn't exist and that Playwright is writing the actual one. `Expected` names where the baseline now is, and `Received` where the same picture was saved for this run. Open it, check it looks right, and commit it. The next run passes.

examples.title: A visual change, caught
examples.prompt: After the baseline was committed, the cards' padding in `src/index.css` changed from `16px` to `20px`. Nothing else did, and every other test still passed.
examples.explanation: `17007 pixels (ratio 0.02 of all image pixels) are different` is the verdict: two percent of the page changed. The call log shows what `toHaveScreenshot` did: it disabled animations, waited for fonts, took a screenshot, found it different, waited, and took a second one to make sure the page had stopped changing before failing. Then come the three files: `Expected` is the baseline, `Received` is this run's screenshot, and `Diff` is the picture with the changed pixels in red. Four extra pixels of padding moved every line of text in every card, which a person would notice at once.

steps.title: Debugging and CI
steps.body:
An e2e test fails far from its cause: the message says a button didn't show up, and the reason might be a slow API, a wrong route, or a CSS rule. Playwright records what happened, so you can see the page at the moment it failed instead of guessing.

## Reading a failure

Start with the error. The first example is the network test from part 4 before its timeout was raised. `toHaveText` waited five seconds and found no alert. With every failure, Playwright writes `error-context.md` in `test-results/`, which includes an **ARIA snapshot**, the page as an outline of roles and names, the way a screen reader sees it, at the moment of failure. This is the snapshot from that failure:

```yaml
- banner:
  - link "Trailhead":
    - /url: /
  - navigation "Main":
    - link "Shop":
      - /url: /products
    - link "Cart (0)":
      - /url: /cart
    - link "Log in":
      - /url: /login
- main:
  - heading "All gear" [level=1]
  - text: Search
  - searchbox "Search"
  - status: Loading products…
- contentinfo: Free shipping on orders over $50
```

The last entry in `main` answers the question at once: `status: Loading products…`. The app hadn't failed yet. It was still retrying.

## Tools for seeing what happened

- **UI mode**, `npx playwright test --ui`, opens a window that lists every test, runs them as you choose, and shows each step with a picture of the page before and after it. Most debugging starts here.
- **Headed mode**, `--headed`, shows the real browser while the tests run, instead of running it hidden.
- **The inspector**, `--debug`, pauses before every action so you can step through, and shows which element each locator matched.
- **The trace viewer** opens a **trace**, a recording of one test: every action, every network request, the console, and a snapshot of the page at each step that you can click through and inspect. The config records one when a test is retried. Open it with `npx playwright show-trace` and the trace's path, or from the HTML report.
- **The HTML report**, `npx playwright show-report`, lists every test of the last run with its steps, errors, screenshots, and traces.
- **Codegen**, `npx playwright codegen http://localhost:4173`, opens a browser and writes test code as you click and type, with role-based locators. It's a quick start for a new test, and the code always needs tidying.

## Running in CI

The second example is a GitHub Actions workflow, `.github/workflows/e2e.yml`, that runs every test on each push to `main` and each pull request. It runs inside Playwright's Docker image from part 5, which already has the browsers and the libraries they need, so the screenshots match the committed `-linux` baselines. `npm ci` installs exactly what the lockfile says. `npx playwright test` builds the shop and starts both servers through `webServer`, fresh, since `CI` is set.

When something fails in CI, you can't open UI mode on the CI server, so the last step uploads `playwright-report/` as an **artifact**, a file the CI service keeps after the job ends. Download it from the job's page and open it with `npx playwright show-report`: it has the failure, the screenshots, and the trace from the retry.

## Flaky tests

A **flaky** test fails now and then with no change to the code. It's the biggest threat to an e2e suite, because once a team learns that red sometimes means nothing, it stops trusting red at all.

The config's `retries: 2` in CI keeps one random failure from blocking a merge, but it hides the problem. Playwright marks a test that failed and then passed on a retry as **flaky** in the report, and that label deserves a bug report, not a shrug. The usual causes:

- **Fixed waits**, like `waitForTimeout`, instead of waiting for what you can see.
- **Shared data**, where two tests running at once change the same cart or product.
- **Tests that depend on order**, passing only after another test has set something up.
- **Things that vary**: the clock, random data, animations, third-party scripts like analytics.
- **Locators that match more than you meant**, which work until the page gains a second match.

To reproduce one, run it many times in a row: `npx playwright test e2e/checkout.spec.ts --repeat-each=20`. Fix the cause, which is almost always one of the above. If it can't be fixed today, mark it `test.fixme`, which skips it with a visible note, and file an issue, so it doesn't slowly teach everyone to ignore the suite.

That's the whole course: Trailhead, built by hand from one component to a tested app. The Next.js course builds the same shop again, with a framework that does much of this work for you.

examples.title: What the page looked like when it failed
examples.prompt: The network test from part 4, with the default five-second timeout. `-g` runs only the tests whose names match.
examples.explanation: The setup project ran first, since the chromium project depends on it, then the test failed after 5.1 seconds. `Locator`, `Expected`, `Timeout`, and `element(s) not found` say what Playwright was waiting for and that it never appeared. The call log lists what it did while it waited, and the source lines point at the assertion. `Error Context` names the file with the ARIA snapshot from this part, the one that showed the app still loading. The fix was a longer timeout for this one assertion, with a comment saying why, rather than a change to the app, since retrying is what the team wants it to do.

examples.title: Running the tests on every push
examples.prompt: `.github/workflows/e2e.yml`. GitHub Actions runs every workflow file in `.github/workflows/`.
examples.code:
name: e2e

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.64.1-noble
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright test
        env:
          HOME: /root
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 14
examples.explanation: `on` says when it runs. `container` runs every step inside Playwright's image, at the same version as the project's `@playwright/test`, so the browsers match without a `playwright install`. `actions/checkout` gets the code and `actions/setup-node` installs Node 24, with npm's download cache saved between runs. `HOME: /root` is a setting Playwright's docs give for Firefox in this image, harmless for Chromium. `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}` uploads the report even when the tests failed, which is when you need it most, and `retention-days` deletes it after two weeks.

recap:
- E2e tests run the real build in a real browser against a real API, so keep them to the journeys that matter.
- Playwright's runner drives browsers, with a fresh context per test and a page as its tab.
- `playwright.config.ts` sets `baseURL`, projects, retries, and `webServer` to start the API and `vite preview`.
- Use role-based locators, let actions auto-wait, use web-first assertions, and never sleep.
- `page.route` stubs, delays, or fails requests, and `waitForResponse` waits for the real ones.
- A setup project logs in once and saves `storageState`, and test data starts from a known seed.
- `toHaveScreenshot` compares against baselines, with masks, disabled animations, and one Docker image for every run.
- Debug with UI mode, traces, and the HTML report, upload the report from CI, and fix flaky tests instead of retrying them.
